notes.meaning: God gave these instructions to Aaron along with Moses because the priests were responsible for carrying them out. The priests had to inspect skin conditions and decide who could enter the sanctuary. Their duty was to protect the holiness of God's dwelling place among the people.

A swelling, a scab, or a bright patch on the skin could be an early sign of an infectious skin disease. Anyone with these marks had to be brought directly to Aaron or another priest for examination. God placed the care of the community's ceremonial cleanliness in the hands of the priests rather than ordinary doctors.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew word translated as skin disease covers many different conditions, including severe rashes and mold, rather than only modern Hansen's disease.

notes.meaning: The priest looked for two specific signs in the sore. If the hair had turned white and the mark reached deeper than the surface of the skin, a serious disease was present. The priest then declared the person unclean, which meant they were barred from worship and camp life until restored.

When a spot was white but not sunken and the hair had not changed color, the priest could not be sure of the diagnosis. Rather than making a hasty decision, the priest isolated the person for seven days. This waiting period kept others safe while allowing time to see how the spot would develop.

If the sore had not changed or spread after one week, the priest ordered a second seven-day isolation. When the second week passed and the sore had faded without spreading, the priest declared the person clean. It was only an ordinary rash, so the person washed their clothes and returned to normal community life.

A person who was declared clean still had to return to the priest if the rash began to spread across the skin. A growing sore proved that a harmful disease was active after all. The priest then declared the person unclean to prevent further defilement in the camp.

A white swelling that turned the hair white and contained open, raw flesh was a clear case of chronic skin disease. Because the signs were unmistakable, the priest did not need to isolate the person for observation. The priest declared the person unclean on the spot.

If a white scaly outbreak spread over the entire body from head to foot, the priest declared the person clean. When the whole surface turned white, the disease had run its course and was no longer an active, running ulcer. Because the outbreak was dry and complete, it posed no danger to the community.

The presence of raw, open flesh showed that the skin was still breaking down and the disease was active. As soon as the priest saw raw flesh, he had to pronounce the person unclean. This protected the people from contact with an ongoing infection.

When the raw flesh healed over and turned completely white, the person returned to the priest. The priest examined the healed skin and declared the person clean. Once the open sore was gone, the person was free to return to the community.

An ordinary boil might heal, but a dangerous infection could start in the damaged skin. If a white swelling or reddish spot formed where the boil had been, the person had to see the priest. If the spot was sunken and the hair turned white, the priest declared the person unclean.

If the spot in the healed boil showed no white hair and was not deeper than the skin, the priest quarantined the person for seven days. If it spread during that time, it was judged to be a contagious disease and declared unclean. If it stayed unchanged, the priest declared the person clean because it was only a normal scar.

A burn from fire could also become infected with a serious skin disease. If the damaged area grew into a reddish-white or white spot that sank deeper than the skin with white hair, it was an outbreak. The priest examined the sore and pronounced the person unclean.

When a burn showed no white hair, was not sunken, and began to fade, the priest isolated the person for seven days. If the mark spread, the priest declared it an infectious disease and the person unclean. If it did not spread and continued to fade, the priest pronounced the person clean because it was only a burn scar.

These instructions applied to infections on parts of the body with thicker hair, such as the scalp or chin of a man or woman. If the sore appeared deeper than the skin and caused the hair to become thin and yellow, it was an infectious scaly outbreak. The priest declared the person unclean because the roots of the hair were affected.
